analysis.one_liner: Protects retirees' company health benefits from being cut and lets them buy continuation coverage until Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee in October 1997 and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would do two things. First, when a company cuts or ends the health benefits it promised retirees, courts would have to order the company to keep paying those benefits while the lawsuit is pending, and the company would bear the burden of proving it clearly reserved the right to cut them. Second, retirees and their spouses whose retiree health plan is substantially reduced or eliminated could keep buying group health insurance under the same continuation rules that already protect laid-off workers, until they qualify for Medicare.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees, disabled former employees, and their spouses and dependents who lose or see reduced employer-sponsored health coverage. Early retirees under 65, who are too young for Medicare and often priced out of individual insurance, would get the option to keep buying group-rate coverage until Medicare eligibility.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees who lost employer health coverage

how_it_helps.text: When a company ends or cuts retiree health benefits and retirees sue, the court would have to order benefits maintained at pre-cut levels while the case is pending, with no bond required from retirees, unless the company proves by clear and convincing evidence the suit is clearly without merit.

If the plan's summary description given to employees was silent or ambiguous about whether retiree benefits could later be cut, the company would have to prove it disclosed this prominently, at least 90 days before retirement, and did not promise lifetime benefits, before terminating coverage.

Retirees and their dependents whose retiree group health plan is substantially reduced or eliminated would gain a qualifying event allowing COBRA-style continuation coverage, purchasable until they become eligible for Medicare.
Employee representatives, such as unions, could bring or appear in lawsuits on behalf of retired employees, their spouses, or dependents.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and plan sponsors, who could no longer freely cut promised retiree health benefits and would bear litigation costs when they try, plus insurers and plans offering the extended continuation coverage; retirees would pay premiums for any continuation coverage they elect.

drawbacks.text: The maintenance-of-benefits rule forces employers to keep paying benefits during litigation even before a court decides the merits, which imposes immediate, potentially unrecoverable costs on employers, including smaller firms facing genuine financial distress.

Extending continuation coverage to retirees adds new coverage obligations and administrative work for group health plans and employers, and retirees must pay the full premiums themselves for the continuation coverage to be of use.
The burden-of-proof shift applies to lawsuits pending or brought on or after January 1, 1998, meaning it would reach plans and employers already operating under prior assumptions about their rights.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For retirees who spent careers counting on promised health coverage, the bill addressed a real and expensive gap: companies could and did cut retiree benefits after retirement, and pre-Medicare retirees often had no affordable alternative. The costs fall on employers and plans, who could face continued obligations during litigation and stricter disclosure standards, though the bill did not ban benefit reductions outright and allowed retirees' premiums to be charged. It would have tilted the rules toward people who relied on promises their employers later changed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to its Labor and Human Resources Committee in October 1997, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Daschle introduced the bill on October 22, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
Four senators, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill.
The only subsequent action was a second set of sponsor introductory remarks in March 1998; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health plans keep the ability to cut or end retiree health benefits and face no new continuation-coverage obligations; retirees who lose employer coverage are left to find insurance on their own.

for.name: Sen. Thomas Daschle
for.role: Senate Minority Leader and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 22, 1997, and delivered introductory remarks on its behalf.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired in the 105th Congress by Sen. Jim Jeffords
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in October 1997 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; no further action followed.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, which remained under the committee and the leader's scheduling control.

sides.party_line_note: All five senators attached to the bill were Democrats; no Republican supported it on the record, and it died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Employers and group health plan sponsors
industries.note: The bill would have restricted their ability to cut or end retiree health benefits by forcing them to maintain benefits during litigation and by shifting the burden of proof to them when plan documents were unclear. It imposed costs but did not prohibit reductions outright.

Extending continuation coverage to retirees creates a pool of premium-paying customers through COBRA and individual-market plans, but individual-market coverage bought by pre-Medicare retirees is typically expensive and the plans take on new administrative duties.
